planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; this old French selection is grown for its distinct foliage rather than a reduced size, so give it the same full-size footprint as the species.

directions: One of the oldest named forms of Southern magnolia still in the nursery trade, Angustifolia predates the 19th century and is distinguished chiefly by its noticeably narrower, lance-shaped leaves with wavy margins and a heavy cinnamon-colored felting on the undersurface. It otherwise grows into a full-size pyramidal tree much like the species, so it suits a spacious lawn, screen planting, or specimen site rather than a tight residential bed. The narrow foliage gives the canopy a finer, more refined texture than broad-leaved cultivars, which is the main reason collectors and specialty growers keep it in circulation. Grow it in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun for the densest branching and best leaf color.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; this historic European selection has been grown as a large specimen or wall-trained tree since the eighteenth century and benefits from a sheltered site in its coldest hardiness zones.

directions: Named for the Marquis de la Galissonnière, who is credited with sending Southern magnolia seed to France in the 1740s, this is one of the earliest named selections grown in European gardens and long predates most American cultivars. It forms a dense pyramidal crown with glossy leaves backed in russet brown, and a related early-flowering strain sold as 'Galissoniensis Praecox' is prized for blooming heavily at a younger age than typical seedling trees. In the garden it performs as a classic full-size Southern magnolia, valued today mainly by collectors and historic-garden plantings for its documented pedigree and dense, formal habit. Give it full sun and fertile, well-drained soil, and allow it the same generous footprint as the wild species.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the exceptionally narrow profile suits tight side yards and street plantings where a standard Southern magnolia's wide crown would not fit.

directions: Emory is grown for an unusually narrow, upright silhouette that is more slender than better-known columnar selections, making it one of the tightest-growing forms of Southern magnolia available. Dark green leaves with brown-felted undersides clothe the tall, slim crown, and the medium, bowl-shaped flowers appear against that narrow backdrop rather than spreading across a wide canopy. Its tight footprint makes it useful as a living screen or accent along a property line or narrow courtyard where a full-spreading Southern magnolia would quickly overwhelm the space. Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained soil, and avoid crowding, since good air movement through the dense, upright branching helps keep foliage healthy.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in spring or fall in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; the unusually large flowers show best on an open-grown specimen with room to develop its broad, compact crown.

directions: Introduced by a French nursery in the mid-1800s, Gloriosa is grown chiefly for flowers that run noticeably larger than those of the species or most later American cultivars, opening wide and heavy on a broad-leaved, comparatively compact crown. The habit is bushier and somewhat less towering than seedling-grown Southern magnolia, which lets the oversized blooms read as the dominant feature of the tree rather than being lost in a tall canopy. It remains a specialty selection grown by collectors and historic plant collections more than a mainstream landscape tree, valued for its documented nineteenth-century origin and flower size. Grow it in full sun and fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil for the fullest bloom display.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun; the vigorous upright habit needs room to reach full size, so site it as a specimen or screen rather than a foundation planting.

directions: Selected in Oregon in the early 1970s, Ruff is grown mainly for leaf undersides that felt out in the darkest, richest red-brown of any widely cited Southern magnolia cultivar, a trait that shows to best advantage whenever wind lifts the glossy green foliage. Growth is vigorous and strongly upright, building a dense pyramidal crown that reaches full species-scale size over time rather than staying compact. Florists and growers who prize magnolia foliage for wreaths and arrangements single this cultivar out for the depth of its indumentum color against the dark green leaf face. Plant it in full sun in moist, fertile, well-drained soil and allow it the same generous mature footprint as a seedling Southern magnolia.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; a little relief from the hottest afternoon sun helps prevent scorch on the lighter, variegated leaf tissue.

directions: Documented since the early twentieth century, Variegata is the long-standing novelty form of Southern magnolia, its glossy evergreen leaves irregularly blotched and streaked with creamy yellow rather than the uniform deep green of the species. The pattern is most pronounced on younger growth and can fade somewhat on older leaves, so the overall effect is a tree that reads as flecked and two-toned rather than crisply bordered like some variegated shrubs. Because reverted, plain-green shoots can appear over time, it benefits from occasional pruning back to the most strongly marked wood to keep the variegation prominent. Grow it in full sun to light shade in moist, fertile, well-drained soil as a conversation-piece specimen rather than a uniform screening tree.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; because it is a female holly, a male American holly nearby improves fruit set.

directions: Howard is a long-grown American holly selection valued for leaves that are nearly free of the sharp marginal spines typical of the species, so plantings along walkways and seating areas are far more comfortable to be near while still delivering the classic dark green, glossy winter foliage. Its habit is dense and columnar, noticeably more compact than a seedling-grown American holly, and it sets abundant bright red fruit on a female plant pollinated by any nearby male holly. The tighter, more tree-like form makes it a practical choice for screening or specimen planting on sites too small for the full-size species. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, and avoid heavy foot-traffic compaction over the root zone.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; as a female cultivar it needs a male American holly within pollinating range to produce its winter fruit crop.

directions: Delia Bradley grows into a strongly upright, pyramidal tree with the typical spiny dark green foliage and conical crown of American holly, carried in good proportion rather than the sprawling, open habit some seedling trees develop. Its chief landscape value is reliability of form and fruit, holding a tidy pyramidal silhouette as it reaches full size while still producing a dependable crop of winter berries on a nearby-pollinated female. It suits use as a specimen tree, background evergreen, or anchor planting at the back of a mixed shrub border where its height and classic holly texture read well year-round. Grow it in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and mulch to keep the shallow root zone cool and evenly moist.

common_name: Steward's Silver Crown Variegated American Holly

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; a male American holly nearby is needed for this female selection to set its winter fruit.

directions: Steward's Silver Crown is grown for a creamy white edge banding the margin of every leaf, a variegation pattern that keeps the plant looking frosted year-round against the deep green leaf centers and gives it a far more ornamental winter presence than plain-leaved American holly. Underneath the showy foliage it behaves like a typical American holly, forming a pyramidal evergreen tree that, as a female selection, carries red berries when pollinated by a male holly nearby. The light leaf margins make a strong accent against dark-foliaged evergreens or a brick or dark-painted wall, where the variegation reads clearly from a distance. Plant in moist, acidic, well-drained soil and give it full sun to partial shade, since too much shade can dull the crisp white edging.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this self-fertile female sets its distinctive fruit without a separate pollinator nearby.

directions: D'Or is the golden-fruited counterpart to the familiar red-berried Burford holly, discovered as a single yellow-fruiting branch sport on a Burford plant in Columbus, Georgia in the 1950s and propagated afterward at Callaway Gardens. It carries the same glossy, nearly spineless dark green leaves and dense, rounded-to-upright habit as its Burford parent, but its heavy winter crop of large berries ripens to a clear golden yellow instead of red, a striking change of pace against evergreen foliage or alongside red-berried hollies. Like other Chinese holly selections it tolerates heat, drought, and a wide range of soils once established, and it can be left unpruned as a large informal shrub or sheared into a hedge. Plant in full sun to light shade in moist, well-drained soil for the heaviest berry set.
